messages.subject: [amelia] AmeliaView will not open
messages.body_plain:
Hi Melissa,  

It's difficult to know what the problem is without a few more details. What version of R are you using on what operating system? What version of Amelia do you have? You can find the version of Amelia by typing the following at the R command prompt:

packageVersion("Amelia")

The most likely issue is that things are out of date. In that case, you can try to update Amelia by opening R and running the following code:

install.packages("Amelia", repos = "http://cran.r-project.org")
library(Amelia)
AmeliaView()

Hope that helps!

Cheers,
matt.

messages.subject: [amelia] Amelia and constructed nominal variables
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm getting some strange results with Amelia using a number of nominal variables. I want try a few things to get a better understanding of what is going on. In particular I'd like to try dealing with the nominal variables manually by creating a set of dummy variables rather than using the noms option to understand what is?occurring?at each step. I'm a little unclear, though, about how to deal with the results. The Amelia documentation says that it transforms the nominal variables into p-1 dummy variables and then runs the program treating the dummy variables as continuous variables, I understand this part. I'm a little less clear on the transformations to get back to a nominal variable. In particular, the documentation says "These continuously valued imputations will?then be appropriately scaled into probabilities for each of the p possible categories." I'm wondering how to do this, scaling to get probabilities, because when I create a set of dummy
 variables the results are definitely not scaled as probabilities; they include negatives and values greater than 1. I'm also not sure how the omitted group fits in. So basically I'm wondering how I would take the results from an imputed set of dummy variables and transform them into probabilities for each of the outcomes.

Thanks for your help.

Matissa

messages.body_plain:

Is it possible to run one multiple imputation (say m=5) on parallelized 
on different processors. That is not as described in the documentation 
"4.2.2 Combining Multiple Amelia Runs", where different imputed datasets 
are combined via "ameliabind".

(Hopefully) more precisely: we'd be interested if we can run one 
"amelia"-command (with, e.g., m=5) using the computational power of 
multiple processors, each of them having R installed.

Thank you for your efforts.

Best,
Philippe

messages.subject: [amelia] Amelia "parallelized" imputation
messages.body_plain:
Hi Philippe,

I don't believe that multicore support is built into Amelia. Here's a solution using a common multicore package for R.

If you're on a Mac, you have to run R from Terminal for foreach() to work. This is a known problem with OS X.

library(Amelia)
# install.packages("doMC")
library(doMC) # Multi-core package for R

registerDoMC(cores = 2) # Register the number of cores you'll be using. Defaults = max number

x <- runif(100); y <- runif(100); z <- runif(100) # Create some data

x[sample(1:100, 20)] <- NA # Add some missing data
y[sample(1:100, 20)] <- NA

D <- data.frame(x,y,z)

# Impute 100 datasets in parallel
Datasets <- foreach(i=1:100) %dopar%
            {
                set.seed(i)
            	amelia(D, m = 1)
            }

# Combine them all into one Amelia object. There's surely a more elegant way.
# Each Amelia object can be grabbed with Datasets[[#]]
# Each Amelia raw dataset can be grabbed with Datasets[[#]]$imputations[[#]]

CombinedData <- Datasets[[1]] # Add the first Amelia object to the combined data

for(i in 2:length(Datasets))
{
    CombinedData <- ameliabind(CombinedData, Datasets[[i]])
}

Imputed <- foreach(i=1:100, .combine = "ameliabind") %dopar% # Impute 100 datasets in parallel
            {
                amelia(D, m = 1)
            }

works.

However, we try to use a non-Mac and non-Unix "machine" for the 
imputation. Using the package "doParallel", as described, e.g., here:

http://stackoverflow.com/questions/10604555/parallel-for-loop-in-windows

does not work either: here, surprisingly, the command amelia is not 
recognized within the "foreach" part. Without that part it'd be, but 
then, it cannot be used with %dopar%.

What are we doing wrong? Is it possible that amelia is not working with 
"doParallel" in conjunction with "foreach" and %dopar%?.

Thank you for your help.

Best,
Philippe

messages.subject: [amelia] Trouble with lgstc variables?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Alicia,

The "lgstc" transformation only works on values strictly between 0 and 1,
that is, not including 0 and 1 themselves. You can use "noms" or "ords" to
handle binary variables if you are using them as a dependent variable.
Otherwise, you are generally fine imputing these binary variables as
continuous.

Hope that helps!

Cheers,
matt.

University of Rochester

messages.subject: [amelia] imputation on test set using train set parameters
messages.subject_clean: [amelia] imputation on test set using train set parameters
messages.body_plain:
Hello,
 
What's the best way to do test set missing feature imputations using parameters derived from a separate training set?
 
I'm using amelia to impute missing values in data which is an input to a forecasting model.  This model must be trained and tested on completely separate data sets; in order to avoid "cheating," amelia imputation parameters can only be derived from the training data, or at least only from data seen up to the point a prediction is made.
 
One way to do this could be to compute an amelia object on the training set, and then use that object for test set imputation.  To do this, you'd have to hack the object, replacing the "imputations" and "misMatrix" members with the test data and the mask indicating which parts are missing.
 
My questions about this are:
 
1.) Is object hacking the only way, or is there something simpler?
 
2.) Assuming that object hacking is the way to go, should "imputations" contain only one copy of the test data?
 
3.) In general, if an amelia object is reused in this way, how are the multiple imputations used?  For example, what if the object and 3 imputations and the amelia call using it has m=6?
 
Thanks,
 
Scott
 
 
Dr. Scott Otterson
Abteilung Energiemeteorologie und Netzintegration
Fraunhofer IWES

E-Mail: scott.otterson at iwes.fraunhofer.de

messages.subject: [amelia] problematic results with nominal option
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I mentioned a few days ago that I was having some problems with nominal variables. I didn't hear back about how the nominal variables are rescaled, but I have confirmed that there seems to be a serious problem in the imputations of nominal variables. I think I found a similar problem the last time I tried Amelia a few years ago, but at the time I was trying to impute a nominal variable with over 300 possible values (occupation) and so I chalked it up to that. Here I've been trying to impute a much simpler nominal variable and I'm getting similar problems. Basically, when I use the nominal option the imputations vastly underrepresent one category. Furthermore, the underrepresented category always seems to be the most common category, I'm guessing because the most common category is the omitted group when Amelia transforms the data into a set of dummy variables. When I create my own dummy variables instead, the means of the imputed dummy values are
 correct. So, for instance, 33% of people should be in a category then the mean of the dummy variable will be 0.33. But the imputed values for these dummy variables are treated as continuous and therefore include values less than 0 and greater than 1, which cause problems for what want to do next with the data. So it's clear that the dummy variables are estimating on average reasonable values, but something in how these values are then rescaled and transformed into a single nominal outcome is problematic. My guess is that it has to do with how the omitted group is treated and that somehow since it's the residual category people it gets assigned last and not often enough.

I've created a moderately simple example that documents this problem. It's not the simplest of cases because I've been using panel data, but I'm quite confident that the fact that it's panel data is not the cause of the problem, especially because I got exactly the same problem with the cross-sectional occupation dataset I tried a couple of years ago. Detailed documentation of this example, including links to download the actual data, are available in this document:

https://dl.dropbox.com/u/16688607/AmeliaProblem/AmeliaFullDocumentation.pdf


Any insights would be greatly appreciated. I may have to resort back to Stata's MI program, although I run into mlogit convergence problems there.?

Thanks,

Matissa

Hi Christian,

I'm not sure about number two but let me try and offer help on 1 and 3.  

1) Practically speaking, I don't believe number one is something that matters to Amelia. That is, if you tell Amelia to use class id as the cross section then it will do so, using the specified interactions with time, etc. if you wish. So, if your unit of analysis is the class then this seems fine. Having said that, I don't think it's a problem to declare more than two id variables if you also have a student id variable. For example, you might try:

amelia(data, idvars = c("year","classid","studentid")) 

3) I think it's always a good idea to work with data in 'long' format but I'm not sure Amelia cares. You can always try to impute using wide format to test. Generally, though, most basic  procedures in R (like ANOVA) require data in long format so it's a good idea to move it there anyway. This is trivial to do using the package "reshape" (see: http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/reshape/reshape.pdf) 


Others may have better advice, hope this helps a bit!  
cheers,

kyle

messages.subject: [amelia] How to hide the future in time series imputations?
messages.subject_clean: [amelia] How to hide the future in time series imputations?
messages.body_plain:
Hello,
 
How can I do imputation on a completely separate future test set, without also using that data to train Amelia parameters?
 
My time-series forecasting model must be trained only on data seen in the past, and tested only on completely unseen future data.  The problem is that Amelia doesn't make a distinction between test and training; imputation parameters are derived from all data, which would be "cheating."
 
One solution could be to run a full imputation for every time instant (if I have K test samples, I could do K Amelia runs, increasing the number of points I show Amelia by one point into the future for each run, ensuring that Amelia never sees data further into the future.  The main problem with this is that my data is very high dimensional, making the CPU cost of this approach prohibitive.
 
Another apparent solution would be to compute an amelia object on the training set, and then use that object for test set imputation by passing it in as an Amelia input.  To do this, I tried hacking the training object, replacing the "imputations" and "missMatrix" object members with the appropriate test data.  The problem is that Amelia then seems to update the imputation parameters, which would again be cheating.
 
Any advice?
 
Thanks,
 
Scott

Amelia currently does not have any functionality that you describe. The
closest approximation is the "overimpute" function, which performs
cross-validation of the imputation model, dropping one observation and
imputing it to see how the model performs. We don't have a way to do
arbitrary training/test set validation. I've added this as a feature
request, so we'll look into how feasible it is.

Amelia does not currently have the ability to incorporate this kind of
"structural" dependence into the imputation algorithm. You could, however,
go into the imputed datasets and edit these inconsistencies by changing
each of that person's "gender" variable to the imputed mode gender value.

observation per child, not per child-year) format. This would only impute
one value of gender for each child.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Christian,

1. My individual data are clustered students in classes, I will
> conduct multilevel models or at least account for the data structure
> with TYPE=COMPLEX in Mplus. Is the cs=classid the right option?
>

Yes, you can use the argument cs = "classid" to set the cross-sectional
variable. Since there is no time-series variable, you should set ts = 0 and
intercs = TRUE, so that only the cross-sectional information will enter the
imputation.



> 2. Are there any information available on how Amelia account for the
> clustered data structure? I just find the information it does, but no
> further details.
>

With the above options, Amelia will include fixed effects (that is, classid
dummies) in the imputation to allow for varying classid intercepts.



>
> 3. Regarding longitudinal data: The data has to be in long format right?
>

Yes, long format is correct.

Cheers,
matt.

messages.subject: [amelia] subsetting imputed datasets
messages.body_plain:
Hi Martin,

It depends on what you want to do with the imputed data. With many of the
Amelia package functions, we rely on the data being perserved so it is
important that the output remain unchanged. That said, many of the
diagnostic functions will accept a "subset" argument so that you can run
them on a subset of each of the imputed dataset. Furthermore, there are
"subset" arguments that you can pass to Zelig functions as well. On the
other hand, if you are passing these imputations to Zelig, it should be
fine to loop in the way that you say, since the Zelig functions do not use
most of the Amelia class structure, just the data.

Hope that helps!

Cheers,
matt.

messages.subject: [amelia] problematic results with nominal option
messages.body_plain:
Hi Matissa,

I worked through your example and I think there is just a bit of confusion
about how we impute nominal variables in Amelia. For the nominal variable
in this case, `MIsimple`, it will do the following steps:

* covert `MIsimple` into 3 binary variables (since there are four
categories and we need an omitted group)
* impute those binary variables using the typical procedure Amelia
procedure (treating them as normal)
* after the imputations, use the 3 imputed values (which are continuous)
for each observation to calculate a probability for each category in each
observation (we do this by scaling and normalizing the imputations to be
between 0 and 1 and to sum up to 1).
* take a draw from a discrete distribution based on the probabilities
calculated in the last step.

Your alternative procedure only does the first two steps above: creates
binary variables and imputes them. But the means of these imputed values
are not necessarily the relative proportion of the sample that is in that
category. This is because the imputations of the binary variables do not
consider the fact that each observation can only have one of these
categories. This is why we must do the third and fourth steps above.

Hope that clarifies things a bit.

Cheers,
matt.

~~~~~~~~~~~
Matthew Blackwell
Assistant Professor of Political Science
University of Rochester
url: http://www.mattblackwell.org
